baseline: Host LTP 20260529 setpriority02 is 7/7 TPASS. Per assertion, the correct kernel returns: (1) setpriority(-1, 0, -2) -> EINVAL, `which` is not PRIO_PROCESS/PRIO_PGRP/PRIO_USER; (2) setpriority(0, -1, -2) -> ESRCH; (3) setpriority(1, -1, -2) -> ESRCH; (4) setpriority(2, -1, -2) -> ESRCH, no process matches `who` for any of the three `which` values; (5) setpriority(0, 0, -2) as uid nobody -> EACCES, target is the caller itself so the ownership check passes and the failure is the RLIMIT_NICE ceiling (init RLIMIT_NICE=0 => lowest permitted nice is 20-0=20, i.e. no negative nice) rejecting the attempt to lower nice to -2; (6) setpriority(1, 0, -2) as uid nobody -> EACCES, same, via the caller's own process group; (7) setpriority(0, 1, -2) as uid nobody -> EPERM, target is pid 1 whose uid/euid are both root while the caller's euid is nobody, and the caller holds no CAP_SYS_NICE, so it is refused before the nice ceiling is ever consulted. The ordering is the load-bearing part: EPERM (may I touch this target at all) is decided strictly before EACCES (may I lower nice this far), so a target the caller does not own reports EPERM even though the RLIMIT_NICE ceiling would also have been violated.
failing_assertion: setpriority02.c:73: TFAIL: setpriority(0, 1, -2) as unprivileged user should fail with EPERM: EACCES (13) -- Asterinas returns -EACCES where Linux returns -EPERM. This is tcases[6] {PRIO_PROCESS, INIT_PID=1, NEW_PRIO=-2, EPERM, unprivil=1}, the only failing subtest; the other 6 pass. Asterinas result 6 pass / 1 fail vs host 7 pass / 0 fail.
root_cause: sys_set_priority (kernel/src/syscall/set_priority.rs:13-45) contains no ownership/credential check at all -- there is no euid, ruid, EPERM or CapSet reference anywhere in the file. It resolves the target set via PriorityTarget::new + get_processes (both in get_priority.rs, which only produce EINVAL for a bad `which` and ESRCH for an empty target set), then for each target process reads that process's own RLIMIT_NICE and returns EACCES at line 36 when new_nice < limit. Because RLIMIT_NICE is initialised to 0 for every process (kernel/src/process/rlimit.rs:20, 69-70) and is inherited, the limit converts to nice 0 for pid 1 as well, so any negative prio trips the line 35 comparison. The unprivileged child therefore reaches the RLIMIT_NICE arm for a target it has no business touching, and the first error it can produce is EACCES. Linux decides the two in the opposite order: set_one_prio calls set_one_prio_perm first and maps false to -EPERM, and only then evaluates `niceval < task_nice(p) && !can_nice(p, niceval)` for -EACCES. Asterinas has only the second half of that pair, so EPERM is unreachable through this syscall -- the errno is not merely mis-ordered, the entire ownership check is absent. Note the EACCES arm is also independently wrong about privilege (Linux's can_nice grants CAP_SYS_NICE holders a bypass of the RLIMIT_NICE ceiling, which Asterinas does not implement), but that half is not what this test observes: root never lowers nice in setpriority02, so it stays out of scope.
invariant: Before a process's scheduling priority may be altered on behalf of a caller, the caller must be authorised to act on that target: its euid must equal the target's real or effective uid, or it must hold CAP_SYS_NICE in the target's user namespace. A caller that fails this test is refused with EPERM, and that refusal is decided before any resource-limit check on the requested priority value, so an unauthorised caller reports EPERM rather than the EACCES that the limit check would have produced.
owning_layer: The process-credential permission layer, alongside the existing check_signal_perm in kernel/src/process/kill.rs:161-202 -- i.e. a shared 'may this thread act on that process' predicate over PosixThread credentials, not an inline test in one syscall body. Asterinas has no equivalent of Linux's set_one_prio_perm, but it does already have this shape twice: check_signal_perm (kill.rs:161) and check_rlimit_perm (syscall/prlimit64.rs:97-133), both of which compare caller credentials against target credentials and then fall back to lsm_hooks::on_capable(CapableContext::new(target_process.user_ns()..., ctx.posix_thread, CapSet::<X>)). The check belongs at that layer and must be applied per target process inside the get_processes loop, because PRIO_PGRP and PRIO_USER fan out to sets whose members can have differing credentials -- placing it once at the syscall entry against `who` would silently authorise every other member of the group. Concretely the check must sit in set_priority.rs's loop above the RLIMIT_NICE arm at lines 31-37, but written as a reusable credential predicate rather than an inline euid comparison, since the sibling schedulers named in other_callers need the identical rule.
linux_reference: kernel/sys.c. set_one_prio_perm(struct task_struct *p) returns true iff uid_eq(pcred->uid, cred->euid) || uid_eq(pcred->euid, cred->euid) || ns_capable(pcred->user_ns, CAP_SYS_NICE); its sole caller set_one_prio maps a false return to -EPERM and only afterwards evaluates `if (niceval < task_nice(p) && !can_nice(p, niceval)) error = -EACCES;`. Both helpers live in kernel/sys.c, i.e. in the generic syscall/process-credential layer, not in the scheduler (kernel/sched/core.c) -- Linux deliberately enforces authorisation above set_user_nice() so every entry point that changes another task's priority shares one rule. That placement is the reference for the owning_layer choice above: Asterinas should likewise enforce it in a credential-layer helper reached by all priority-setting syscalls, not inside sched. niceval is also clamped into [MIN_NICE, MAX_NICE] before either check, matching what Asterinas already does at set_priority.rs:16-19, so an out-of-range prio is never itself an error.
other_callers: The defect is reachable only through sys_set_priority today -- sys_get_priority is a read and needs no such check, and Asterinas implements no sys_nice (syscall 34 in the x86 table at kernel/src/syscall/arch/x86.rs:219 is sys_pause; there is no SYS_NICE entry in either arch table), which in Linux is the other route into set_one_prio. So for the target test a fix confined to set_priority.rs is defensible. But the same missing rule is present in the sibling scheduling syscalls, which is why the predicate should be shared rather than inlined: sys_sched_setattr, sys_sched_setscheduler and sys_sched_setparam all route through access_sched_attr_with (kernel/src/syscall/sched_getattr.rs:197-214), which resolves an arbitrary tid from the pid table and applies the new policy with no credential check whatsoever -- grepping kernel/src/syscall/sched_*.rs for credentials or CapSet returns nothing. sys_ioprio_set (kernel/src/syscall/set_ioprio.rs) has the same gap for I/O priority, where Linux likewise requires CAP_SYS_NICE. Those are pre-existing and out of scope for this run, but a fix written as an inline euid comparison inside set_priority.rs leaves them unfixable without a second refactor. Within set_priority.rs itself, the fan-out arms matter: PRIO_PGRP and PRIO_USER iterate multiple processes, so the check must be per process.
suggested_direction: Add a credential-layer predicate for priority changes, modelled on check_signal_perm (kernel/src/process/kill.rs:161-202) and check_rlimit_perm (kernel/src/syscall/prlimit64.rs:97-133): given the calling PosixThread and a target Process, return Ok(()) when the caller's euid equals the target main thread's ruid or euid, else when lsm_hooks::on_capable(CapableContext::new(target_process.user_ns().lock().as_ref(), ctx.posix_thread, CapSet::SYS_NICE)) succeeds (CapSet::SYS_NICE already exists at kernel/src/process/credentials/capabilities.rs:34 and is currently referenced nowhere else), and otherwise EPERM. Call it inside the `for process in processes.iter()` loop in sys_set_priority, positioned above the RLIMIT_NICE arm at lines 31-37 so EPERM strictly precedes EACCES. Two things to preserve: subtests 5 and 6 must stay EACCES, which they will because the target there is the caller's own process (and its own group), so euid == ruid and the predicate passes through to the limit check; and subtests 1-4 must stay EINVAL/ESRCH, which they will because PriorityTarget::new and get_processes run before the loop is entered. Do not relocate the RLIMIT_NICE logic or touch the FIXME at lines 38-40 about fair-scheduler thread state -- setpriority01 depends on that and is deliberately out of scope. Placing the predicate in the credential layer rather than inline also leaves the sched_setattr/sched_setscheduler/sched_setparam and ioprio_set gaps fixable by later work without re-deriving the rule.
